_note: Scenario content for the Brayford Stores journey. Every figure here is either computed from data/standards.json or quoted from the source named in `source`. Nothing in this file is invented except the fictional employer and its ten people.

employer.name: Brayford Stores
employer.payBillNote: 1340 staff at the UK average salary of £40,911. The levy is charged on the whole pay bill — not just salaries above a threshold — so it is usually a bigger number than employers expect.

payBillFrom.source: ONS Annual Survey of Hours and Earnings, published 22 October 2026
payBillFrom.definition: Median gross annual earnings for FULL-TIME employees who had been in their job for at least a year, April 2026 (provisional).
payBillFrom.caveat: That definition excludes part-time staff and anyone under a year in post. A real retail chain of this size carries a lot of both, so its pay bill per head would be lower and this makes Brayford a better-paying employer than most of its sector. The figure is used because it is the published national average and can be checked; the page says so rather than quietly picking a number that suits the story.

verified.standards: Skills England apprenticeships export, accurate as of 28 June 2026, checked against the live standard pages 2026-11-03

pathway.modelNote: Competent at two years, senior at five. Training occupies two of those five years; the rest is time in role.

instances.label: Business administrator L3 — junior management pathway
instances.soldAsNote: Providers package this standard as a management foundation programme, which is how the gap left by Team leader L3 is being filled. The levy buys the standard. Leadership extras sit outside it.

markers.label: Competent
markers.note: Qualified, and six months into doing the job unsupervised.

markers.label: Senior
markers.note: Training finished at year four. The last year is earning it in role, not sitting a course.

options._note: Five standards shown, TWO selectable. The other three are each unsuitable for a different reason, and the page gives the reason rather than hiding the option: one cannot be bought, one is the wrong discipline, one is a sideways move. A list that quietly dropped them would teach nothing - these are the three a real employer actually reaches for.

list.variantNote: The standard is Business administrator. “Junior management pathway” is how providers package it — the leadership content, the CMI route and the masterclasses are wrapped around the standard, and sit outside the levy. The levy buys the standard; the certificate says administration.

list.why: The obvious first step into managing, and it was until 1st September 2026. New starts are no longer government funded, so your levy contributes nothing and the whole cost falls on you while the account sits full.

A good standard for a different job. Three times the band, nine months longer, and it qualifies them in Digital while the shop floor still has nobody trained to run it. This is the one a board asks for.

Funded, in your sector, and the cheapest on the list, which is exactly why it gets picked. But it develops the job they already do rather than the one they are moving into - it deepens customer service, it does not start anyone managing. Cheapest is not the same as a step up.

ksb._note: Area headings as published, with the opening words of each statement. Quoted from the standard pages listed in `source`; full text is on those pages. Used to compare what each standard actually covers against what a first-line retail manager does. The `manages` flag is OUR classification of whether an area is about managing people or money, not something the published standard states. It is shown as a judgement on screen, not as a fact from the source.

coverage._note: Which of the six management areas each person's CURRENT job description evidences, and which line of it is the evidence. `jd` indexes that person's jd array. Anything absent is "not in the job description" - a claim about the JD, not about the person.
coverage._method: READ, not scored. A keyword overlap between these JDs and the published KSBs finds management vocabulary in only 2 of 60 person-area pairs, and misses a checkout supervisor who sets rotas and holds absence conversations, because the standard says "recruit, retain and develop" where her JD says "return-to-work conversations". Same duty, no shared words. The page states that this mapping is a judgement and shows the evidence line beside every claim so a reader can disagree with it.
coverage._areas: The six are the areas of the published Retail manager standard that WE classify as being about managing people or money. That classification is ours, not the standard's.
_revisions: Jordan A. Leadership partly -> yes: the same act as Dan F., who was already marked yes. Consistency, not a loosening.
Priya N. Communication partly -> yes: a daily team brief is cascading information. Both reads are defensible; the evidence line is shown so a reader can take the other one.

Jordan A.: his JD line “allocate the backroom team” was rewritten to “sequence put-away against replenishment priorities”. The scenario needed five colleagues who cannot be put forward; changing the authored role is honest, re-scoring the same words to a different answer would not be. The Leadership entry went with the line it rested on.

ratio.targetNote: A voluntary employer charter, not a statutory ratio. Members aspire to 5% of their UK workforce in “earn and learn” positions within five years of joining, with Gold awarded at 5% and Platinum at 10% per the club’s 2025 audit guidance.
ratio.targetCaveat: IMPORTANT: the 5% covers earn-and-learn BROADLY — apprentices, sponsored students and graduates on formalised schemes — not apprenticeships alone. So the headcount target is wider than an apprenticeship cohort, and a cohort is a share of it rather than the whole of it. Sources also disagree on the tier bands; the club’s own audit document is the one used here.
ratio.ceilingNote: Applied at DEPARTMENT level, not across the workforce. 30% of a chain is 402 people and never binds; 30% of a team of three is one person and binds immediately. This is the author’s operating rule, not a published standard, and the page attributes it that way.
ratio.ceilingOwner: the author's operating rule, not a published standard

ksbFull._codes: ST0070 publishes NAMED competency areas, not K1/S1/B1 codes. The codes here are positional so the report can label rows, and the report says so. The counts are real: 8 Knowledge, 8 Skills, 5 Behaviours, 21 in total.
ksbFull._method: Each mark is a judgement, read from the colleague’s job description against the published statement, and carries the JD line that justifies it. Absent means "not evidenced in the job description" — a claim about the JD, not about the person. The threshold used for the verdict band is the 50% guidance line, which is a convention rather than a funding rule.

items.text: The company's purpose, activities, aims, values, vision, resources, and how political and economic conditions affect it.
The company's structure, how their own work benefits it, where they fit in their team, and how their skills support progression.
Managing relationships with internal and external customers, clients, suppliers and partners.
Laws and rules that apply to the role, such as data protection, health and safety and compliance.
Internal company policies and the key business policies for the sector.
Principles such as managing change, business finance and project management.
Workflows such as payments and customer data handling, suggesting improvements, and handling billing and purchase orders.
External influences such as market forces, policy and regulatory change, and supply chains, and their business impact.
Using relevant software and systems for correspondence, proposals, financial processes and data.
Producing accurate records and documents, recommending improvements, and handling confidential information.
Using sound judgement, handling challenges maturely, and seeking advice from experienced colleagues.
Building positive working relationships, influencing others, and acting as a role model.
Communicating effectively in person, by phone, in writing and online, and representing the organisation.
Producing high-standard work, reviewing processes for improvement, and resolving complex complaints.
Managing tasks, priorities and deadlines, organising meetings, and managing resources and logistics.
Applying project management principles and tools to scope, plan, monitor, report on and lead projects.
Behaving professionally, respecting diversity, following the code of conduct, representing team culture.
Integrity, reliability, self-motivation, proactivity and a positive attitude.
Taking responsibility for their own work and development, accepting feedback, and self-assessing.
Adjusting to changing priorities in their own work and in the organisation.
Taking ownership of team performance and project quality, and developing their own and others' skills.

providerLinks.disclosure: These go to the government’s own provider directory, not to anyone’s sales page. No provider named there is affiliated with this site, recommended by it, or paying to appear. Listings are live and change — provider counts, achievement rates and availability move constantly, and nothing here is checked for currency after the date above.
providerLinks.whyNotDirect: Linking one provider’s programme would read as an endorsement on a page that argues their management wrap sits outside the levy, and provider pages rot. The directory shows everyone delivering the standard, with achievement rates, and stays current on its own.

units.name: Apprenticeship units
units.sourceName: Apprenticeship unit technical funding guide, GOV.UK
facts: Short, flexible training courses available from April 2026, built from employer-led occupational standards — job-specific skills rather than a whole occupation.
30 to 140 hours, delivered across 1 to 16 weeks.
Paid from your employer account, up to the funding rate — the same pot as a full apprenticeship.
Government funds all the training and assessment cost, up to the funding rate.
For a learner aged 25 or over, government funds 75% and you pay 25%, for units starting on or after 1 August 2026. Earlier starts attracted 95%. Learners aged 19 to 24 are fully funded.
units.whyHere: A unit is the obvious move for someone a year away from a full standard. It is weeks rather than eighteen months, it comes from the same levy you are already paying, and it can target the exact duties their job does not yet cover — so they arrive at next year’s cohort with the evidence already built.
